newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Consortium mulls high-tech oil drilling in Africa.
newsitem.headline: Consortium mulls high-tech oil drilling in Africa.

text.p: Deep water oil drilling off Ivory Coast, billed as a 21st century opportunity, is not likely to begin until 1998 when analysis of seismic tests would be completed, a consortium partner said on Wednesday.
Houston-based United Meridian Corp, which is a partner in the high-tech venture with Shell Exploration Africa BV, said it would take at least six months to process preliminary data collected.
"A boat completed seismic spots late last year and it will take about six to seven months to process," Meridian's Chief Operating Officer James Dunlap told Reuters.
"After that we have to agree what steps to take, on the assumption we are still high on prospection targets," he said.
UMIC and Shell signed a contract with the Ivory Coast government last September for the West African country's first deepwater offshore block.

UMIC and Shell hold a respective 35-percent and 55-percent working interest in Bloc CI-105, also known as Entente, and lying in depths ranging from 500 metres (1,500 feet) to 2,000 metres (6,000 feet). Ivorian national oil company PETROCI is the other consortium partner.
Meridian is the operator in the exploration phase while Shell will be operator in the development and production stage if a discovery is made.
Neither UMIC nor Shell have put a figure on what Dunlap described as "a 21st century opportunity", but investment in technology will be colossal if drilling goes ahead.
"The likely place we will be drilling is 1,400 metres and there may be only a dozen rigs in the world that can drill at that depth," UMIC's President Jim Smitherman told Reuters.
Both Smitherman and Dunlap were in Ivory Coast as part of a U.S. business mission which also visited Equatorial Guinea, where UMIC and Mobil are in joint exploration.
"It will take the world's best technology to drill at that depth, and if oil is found it will be a very expensive development programme," Smitherman said.
"If we don't drill by 1998 probably there will be no production until 2000," he added.
Dunlap said if the first well is successful there will have to be two to three more wells drilled in the concession to know exactly what type of technology will be required.
"We won't know that until sometime next year," he added.
In the meantime conasortium members are delaying any firm decisions on their ultimate exposure.
The Ivory Coast government is not likely to increase its stake through PETROCI, preferring to receive taxes than risk its money in an expensive venture, industry sources say.
UMIC is the only oil firm already producing oil in Ivory Coast, which is pinning its hopes in part on becoming a regional economic power on its offshore oil and gas reserves.

UMIC is currently producing 20,000 barrels per day of oil from the Lion field and associated Lion B-4 and A-4, and 60 million cubic feet a day of gas which largely feeds Ivory Coast Vridi thermal power complex in Abidjan.
UMIC says its gas output is limited only by the market price but more will come on stream to meet expected demand from neighbouring Ghana and a new 100 megawatt Ivorian thermal power plant.
